title: Iran Nears Hormuz Shipping Deal With Oman; Gulf States Set Salalah Summit as IAEA Sends Tehran to UN Security Council
subhead: Tehran says a temporary safe-route agreement for the Strait of Hormuz is days away and Gulf foreign ministers will meet Iran in Oman on Monday, even as the IAEA board referred Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council for the first time in two decades — two tracks that will shape the next phase of the crisis.

sections.heading: Iran Says Hormuz Shipping Deal With Oman Is Days Away
sections.body:
Iran said a deal with Oman establishing a temporary safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz is 'days away,' according to Bloomberg and Reuters reporting cited across outlets. The arrangement would cover tanker traffic through the waterway, potentially easing a choke point where tracked vessel crossings have fallen to roughly half their pre-war levels since Iran's blockade and the US-Iran war began in February.

Under the reported terms, Iran and Oman would set a temporary navigation corridor and are also likely to seek service fees from vessels using it, per Bloomberg. Officials signaled the agreement could allow more tankers to transit while giving Tehran a formal role in managing the strait's traffic. Oil markets have traded on the news: Brent extended gains near $104 as traders weighed whether the deal would meaningfully loosen supply or simply formalize Iranian control over what flows.
sections.whyItMatters: This is the first concrete diplomatic instrument proposed to reopen Hormuz, but it is not neutral — it would institutionalize Iran's role as gatekeeper of the world's most important oil artery, with Tehran collecting fees on movement. The market's hesitation reflects that a 'safe route' run by the blockader is a different proposition from a return to free transit.

sections.heading: Gulf States and Iran to Meet in Salalah on Monday
sections.body:
Foreign ministers from Gulf states, alongside representatives from Iraq, will meet Iran on Monday, September 14, in Salalah, Oman to discuss maritime security and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, regional officials said. The summit signals that — even as US-Iran talks remain stalled — Gulf capitals are pursuing a parallel, regional channel with Tehran to manage shipping rather than leaving the strait's fate to Washington and the war.

The meeting comes as the Gulf's export architecture is under strain on multiple fronts: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline was shut this week after a drone strike, Houthi forces now hold Yemen's Red Sea coast near Bab el-Mandeb, and Qatar's LNG exports remain disrupted. A Gulf-Iran arrangement on Hormuz — however limited — would be the first attempt to normalize some level of Gulf energy transit since the blockade began.
sections.whyItMatters: Gulf states opening direct maritime-security talks with Iran, days after the US sank Iranian tankers and bombed the country, reveals a widening gap between Gulf capitals and Washington's approach. The Salalah meeting is a hedge: Gulf producers want the oil flowing even if the war does not end, and they are willing to deal with Tehran to achieve that.

sections.heading: IAEA Sends Iran's Nuclear File to UN Security Council for First Time in 20 Years
sections.body:
The IAEA Board of Governors voted 23-3 to refer Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council, a step not taken in two decades, on a resolution backed by Western nations citing nuclear 'non-compliance,' Reuters and IAEA reporting show. The referral follows Tehran's refusal to allow IAEA inspectors back to several bombed sites, including three uranium enrichment facilities destroyed or heavily damaged in US and Israeli strikes.

Russia and China rejected the move, joining Iran in warning against the Security Council referral, and Moscow and Beijing opposed efforts to reactivate a UN sanctions committee on Iran's nuclear program. The council is expected to weigh a ceasefire resolution pushed by Russia and China even as the referral complicates Tehran's position. This is the first time since roughly 2006 that Iran's nuclear file has been escalated to the Security Council — but in a context where Iran's nuclear infrastructure has already been largely destroyed by war.
sections.whyItMatters: Escalating Iran's file to the UN Security Council while the country's enrichment sites lie in ruins is diplomatically significant but practically limited — there is little left to 'divert' and no inspection regime to restore while the war is active. The referral is therefore more a statement about post-war accountability and the West's legal posture than a lever that can change Iran's behavior now. Russia and China's rejection sets up a Security Council clash over both the referral and their separate ceasefire drive.

sections.heading: Europe Heads Into Winter With Gas Storage at a Near Two-Decade Low
sections.body:
European gas storage is at its lowest level for this time of year in nearly two decades, with the EU entering the heating season about 15 years' low by some measures, per reporting from outlets citing EU data and the Wall Street Journal. Europe is 'losing the battle with Asia for scarce LNG cargoes,' pushing TTF gas and northwest European LNG prices to their highest levels since 2023.

Disrupted Qatari LNG exports — a casualty of the Gulf war — are compounding European storage problems, and analysts warn European wholesale gas prices could top 100 euros this winter, a return to crisis-era levels not seen since the 2022 Russia-Ukraine spike. The EU is planning winter LNG purchases to offset the deficit, while Asian spot LNG prices have hit their highest since end-December 2022 on the same supply squeeze and winter demand.
sections.whyItMatters: With Qatari supply interrupted and Asia outbidding Europe for cargoes, European storage — already depleted heading into autumn — leaves the continent exposed to a brutally expensive winter. The gas picture is now the clearest channel through which the Hormuz war is translating into a cost-of-living shock across Europe, independent of crude prices.

sections.heading: India Turns to Russia for Critical Minerals as Modi-Putin Talks Deepen
sections.body:
During recent Modi-Putin discussions, India signaled it is looking to Russia to plug gaps in critical minerals and rare earths, seeking greater control over sourcing, processing, and value addition, according to regional reporting on the talks. Russia's substantial mineral resource base is positioned as a source New Delhi can draw on as it steps up overseas sourcing of the inputs needed for defense, electronics, and clean-energy supply chains.

The India-Russia critical-minerals track sits alongside a broader set of moves: Australia has offered to sell shares in its new strategic reserve of critical minerals to allies including Britain, while the US signed a critical minerals framework memorandum with Colombia earlier this year — each government scrambling to secure supply chains for lithium, rare earths, and processing capacity as the transition accelerates.
sections.whyItMatters: India leaning on Russia for critical minerals and rare earths deepens Moscow's role as a commodities anchor for the non-Western world, mirroring the oil relationship that has kept Russian crude flowing to India despite sanctions. For Western supply-chain-security planners, India's pivot toward Russia on transition minerals is the same strategic problem they face with China — but through a partner the West has been courting.

sections.heading: Markets: Brent Near $104 as Supply Crunch and Diplomacy Pull Both Ways
sections.body:
Brent traded near $104.6 with WTI around $100.1 and Gulf-grade Murban at a wide premium near $119.5, reflecting the steep repricing of Gulf crude specifically, per OilPrice.com price data. The Iran-Oman shipping story has injected a diplomatic variable into a market that had been pricing a long, expensive shortage.

US shale producer Occidental announced it will not add more oil hedges this year, citing volatility after the Iran war that lowered realized prices — a sign producers are balking at locking in prices in an unstable, war-driven market rather than positioning for a stable recovery. Meanwhile, analysts continue lifting price forecasts: a Reuters poll found the Iran-war shock has driven the steepest hike yet in annual oil price forecasts, with US President Donald Trump predicting oil stays high through the November midterms.
sections.whyItMatters: The market is oscillating between two opposing forces: a supply crunch that has producers refusing to hedge and forecasters raising price calls, and the prospect that a Gulf-Iran navigation deal could start loosening the strait. Until the Salalah summit clarifies whether the safe-route plan is real and enforceable, oil stays pinned near $104 with Gulf grade much higher, pricing that the bottleneck remains unresolved.

bottomLine: The day's defining development is diplomatic: Iran says a temporary Hormuz shipping deal with Oman is days away and Gulf foreign ministers will meet Tehran in Salalah, Oman on Monday — the first concrete effort to reopen the world's key oil artery by negotiation rather than by war's end, even as it would formalize Iranian control over the strait. In parallel, the IAEA board referred Iran's nuclear file to the UN Security Council for the first time in two decades, a move Russia and China rejected, setting up a council clash over accountability even as a ceasefire resolution circulates. Beneath both, Europe is heading into winter with gas storage at a near two-decade low and LNG prices at 2022-level highs, India is deepening its critical-minerals dependency on Russia, and Brent holds near $104 with Gulf crude far higher. The coming week's Salalah summit — not Washington's war — now looks like the most consequential event for energy markets.
sources: Bloomberg, Reuters, OilPrice.com (Charles Kennedy), IAEA, Al Jazeera, Reuters poll, EU data via Wall Street Journal, TRT World, Anadolu Agency, regional reporting on Modi-Putin talks
